chapter: Emmett Hardy, Bix and the Rhythm Kings
title: The Wolverines record and Hardy's drive and style
summary: Hazel played the Wolverines record for Hardy, who identified Bix and Louis Black; he describes Hardy's legato style, New Orleans drive and refusal of Whiteman.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: But, uh, it's, you know, such a shame. Yeah. But, uh, now, uh, another thing, Bill, uh, the first record that ever, that ever came here, of the Wolverines. Nobody knew who the Wolverines, because they didn't, in those days, they didn't have any personnel or anything like that on, on, what's it? Well, I was working for Con Company. And the day, and I had the band at the Bienville Hotel and at the, Roots, where the Blue Room is now. We used to play dinner there, and then go up the Bienville Roof from nine to one, you see. And, uh, they had a, uh, a piano company sharing the building with us, called the Junus Hart Piano Company. And they sold records. Yeah. So, I hear this record, this Wolverines band was on Jeanette. And, uh, the tunes were the Jazz Me Blues, and whatever was on the other side. Oops, I don't get it. Whatever was on the, on the other side of the Jazz Me Blues. Well, I used to, I used to buy records and I'd bring them up to the house and play them for them, you know. And I'd come around, I was all in through it. I'd say, I got one, you don't know who it is. You know, like that. So, I, I put it on, I played it. So, he listened to it. And when he got through he says, uh, I know who that is. I said, who? And no, nobody had ever heard anything of Bix or anything else. I mean, he had told me about meeting Bix up there in Davenport, you know, and about the...
Okay, you played the record for Air Ruffin.

And, uh, he says, I know who that is. So, he told us, that's a kid from Davenport by the name of Bix. He didn't call him Bix, he called him Leon, his right name. Right. So, that's a kid from Davenport by the name of Leon Bodyback. He didn't know who the rest of the band was, because he didn't know any of them. Outside, yeah, he did know that, he knew the banjo player, who was the same banjo player who played with the Wolverines, Louis Black. And, uh, he taught, and the thing, the trumpet solo, well, in fact, the whole arrangement, the thing was note for note the way Emmett used to play it, you see? And, uh, he said, uh, he even told me what key they were playing, you see? And, uh, got the horn and figured out, and they were playing in E flat, I think, a B flat, something like that. He even knew what key, he could listen to a record and tell you what key they were playing in. And, uh, he was another one of those guys like T. Gordon, you know, you go way in the back room and hear the chord, he'd tell you what chord, the notes in the chord, all those things, just like Jack. And, uh, while he was with the Rhythm Kings in Chicago for that month there, he had an offer from Whiteman, and he turned, he turned Whiteman down. And, uh, the guy, nobody, nobody can, unless you heard him play, Bill, nobody could explain it to you. And a lot of people would think, oh, you, you don't know what you're talking about, and things like that. But the guy had what Bix got from him. But the thing that Bix or hack at either one of them, or any other guy that played that style, don't have what he had. He had the New Orleans drive. He had the drive with that beautiful style, that legato style. That's what it is, it's more of a legato style than it is a staccato style. And he had, he had the drive that goes with it, even more than Sharky drives. He had to drive something like, uh, well not as wild, not as wild as Wild Bill, uh, uh, those guys. But it was more of a, more of a, Charlie, Charlie DuPont, when he played Conrad, had to drive, the drive, that's all. That's all he had. He had to drive like, like Emmett had. But he, man, he'd swing a band, you know, to death.
And all that when he was only 21, huh?
He died when he was 21. Now he was sick two years before he died.
